scenes.title: Benin
scenes.subtitle: A history told only by its sources

scenes.caption: Photo 1930 · Porto-Novo
scenes.text: BDArch identified five archaeological phases and three cultural periods prior to Dahomey's rise, with settlement expansion and nucleation occurring from the Yellow Pottery Period (670–540 BC) through the Sodohomé Period (AD…

scenes.caption: Photo 1903 · Cotonou
scenes.text: By AD 1000, clear evidence of small-scale iron smelting appears, expanding by AD 1400 to industrial-scale production.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930 · Cotonou
scenes.text: More than thirty sites have been documented across southern Benin, with induced-draft furnaces and extensive slag heaps indicating massive output—estimated at over four million kilograms of iron between AD 1400 and 1600.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930 · Porto-Novo
scenes.text: From the 1560s, African captives labeled "Aradas" were recorded in Peru, and the city appeared on Portuguese charts after 1570.

scenes.caption: Photo 1902 · Cotonou
scenes.text: It is also possible that the dynasty emerged during the collapse of the iron economy on the plateau around 1600, creating opportunities for new elites to redirect trade toward the coast.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930 · Cotonou
scenes.text: The Dutch West India Company acquired around 800 slaves annually from Allada between 1636 and 1647, and by the 1680s, the Slave Coast exported roughly 5,000 captives per year, increasing to 10,000 by the 1710s.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: On December 4, 1958, it became the Republic of Dahomey.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: By 1975 the Republic of Dahomey changed its name to the People's Republic of Benin.

scenes.caption: Photo 1930
scenes.text: President Kérékou was barred from running under the 1990 constitution due to term and age limitations.

scenes.title: What the sources leave out
scenes.text: Before 670 BC, history is not dated in these sources: oral traditions, archaeology and local sources are still to be brought in.
